div2.head: Scene 1
div2.stage: AT RISE: The COUNT anxiously paces the stage. The DUKE enters. Both are in hunting apparel.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I have left my huntsmen in pursuit of a wild boar, don Duarte, thus affording us the privacy you requested. I cannot fathom, however, for what perturbed and perplexed motive, when I have called this hunt specially to honor your arrival, you wish to leave the chase and speak to me alone.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Enough dissembling. Unsheathe your steel, which, like Numa, that saintly king, you’ve forgotten at your side. The naked blade you see before you, Your Grace, will shortly give my reply. The sword, not the pen, must serve as tongue for the aggrieved gentleman, and mute, it broadcasts your shame.

div2.stage: (Brief sword fight; the DUKE knocks the COUNT’S sword away.)

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: The sword is indeed a tongue, for it resembles one—and since yours has led you to babble baseless accusations, let us hold our tongues and allow our blades to speak for us. Unless you wish to explain yourself in the time I give you, which will be short, as you have been short with me. My honor owes you nothing.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Splendid! You think you can conceal the crimes which heaven itself makes known?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What crimes?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Try as you may try to hide behind your age and dignity, sir, you cannot fool me. The proof is in this letter, signed and sealed by your own hand. (thrusting the letter at the DUKE) Take it—it’s yours. The servant you bribed to kill me is bronze-like in the strength of his loyalty, and your offer could not breach so thick a wall. And seeing as you put your order in writing, you should not wonder when I say you’d rather wield a pen than a sword.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I, order you killed?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: This seal, is it not yours?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: And can you deny this signature?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Am I dreaming this or am I mad?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Read the letter and you’ll see why I seek my revenge.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: (reading) “For the retribution of certain crimes, which may only be satisfied by the death of don Duarte, the Count of Estremoz, I place my trust in you, his personal valet. Prove my trust to be well founded, and act as the agent of my revenge. This accomplished, make haste to my castle, where I will safeguard and reward you for the danger in which you have placed yourself for my sake. Once you have read this letter, return it to the messenger, remembering always the importance of both haste and secrecy. THE DUKE.”

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: I know not what injury the house of Estremoz, of which I am Count, has done you to so debase a noble breast that flows with the ancient blood of the Dukes of Avero.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Some traitor has forged my signature and seal, a man who harbors a secret grievance, and who intends with your death to effect my perpetual disgrace. Heaven, which knows the author of this crime, knows too that never, in presence or in absence, in act, in speech, or in writing, have I ever sought your harm. I’ve a feeling it won’t take long to discover our cowardly author. In the meantime, however, while I confess the justice of your complaint, I beg that you suspend your righteous anger and calm your troubled breast.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: I am contented, Your Grace… for now.

sp.speaker: HUNTER 1
sp.p: What a boar!

sp.speaker: HUNTER 2
sp.p: We went after it, but it had these huge tusks, and even with the hounds on its scent it managed to get away, and—

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: My friends! I’m sure you’ve left not a single deer or boar alive in this forest. How is the catch?

sp.speaker: HUNTER 1
sp.p: Let’s just say your mules won’t be going home with light loads.

p.seg: That dastardly secretary!

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Figueredo! Why are you in such a hurry?

sp.speaker: FIGUEREDO
sp.p: Thank God I’ve found you—treason, Your Grace! A plot hatched by your secretary, Ruy Lorenzo, to kill don Duarte! You owe me your life, sir.

p.seg: I can guess the reason for this secretary’s ill-plotted revenge. I seduced his sister, the beautiful Leonela, and once I’d had my way, I ditched her.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Thank heaven, which justifies the innocent! How was this plot exposed?

sp.speaker: FIGUEREDO
sp.p: The traitor hired a young thug and, for good measure, told him that you, sir, gave the command. But this thug happened to be in love, and men in love, as you know, are as free with their tongues as with their money. They say the bed is a rack where women torture men, not with ropes but with kisses. He told the plan to his mistress and she swore secrecy. Still, whatever a man plants in a woman is bound to come out one way or another. If she conceived through the ear, she gave birth through the mouth, and by noontime everyone in Avero knew. They arrested the thug, but Ruy Lorenzo escaped with his footman.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: You see, don Duarte, how Providence has revealed the truth and proven my innocence.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: I know not what to say—only that your secretary’s deceitful plot was the root of my own too hasty action. Still, who may not be fooled by a false pen?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Henceforth I’ll take more care in my choice of a secretary.

p.seg: Leonela’s revenge is behind all this. Her cause is a just one, so I’ll have to make certain the Duke doesn’t find out.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: For such a traitor, the greatest torture is but little. Whoever brings me the culprit, dead or alive, wins his forfeited estate.

sp.speaker: HUNTER 2
sp.p: Not a soul in the county will fail to take you up on that one, sir.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: His punishment will be an example to all the kingdom.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: I owe you my life, my friend.

div2.head: Scene 2
div2.stage: SETTING: Another part of the forest.
AT RISE: TARSO bursts onstage, pursued by MELISA.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: You’d leave me just like that, you traitor?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Melisa, go bark up someone else’s tree. Your love just doesn’t make me feel the way it used to. It’s been half a year since we were together, and I’ve gotten over whatever illness made me love you. I put my love on a diet, and little by little, I’ve recovered my health. I’m not mad anymore because I’m not a poet anymore. My God, the poems I used to make up for you left and right! I climbed up Mt. Parnassus to borrow words from the Muses themselves, but all I ended up with was blisters on my feet. I called you my “moon,” my “evening star”… There wasn’t a single thing about you whose praises I didn’t sing. I made up couplets about your laugh, your sweet smile, your white skin, your dark eyes, your haughty airs, your silence, your talking, your sighing, your walking, your crying, your sitting, your coughing, your spitting… I think one time I even composed a sonnet about that little drop that hangs off the end of your nose. Now I’ve escaped from the trap you caught me in, thank God, and I don’t give a damn about you or your love.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Tarso, you’re such a… man! How could a little time apart make you lose all your regard for me?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You deserve as much regard as Judas, and you’re about as faithful. Don’t think you can just pretty up your face and expect me to come running back to you.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Fine! Then give me back all those love tokens I gave you, those pretty little ribbons and locks of my hair…

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You think I still keep those in a pouch around my neck like I used to? As if I’d rub salt in the wound. Those locks of hair you used to tie up my hopes, those cruel ribbons, roses, letters, cards… They had me bewitched, so I did what I had to to break the spell: I burned them. I even burned the pouch—it was contaminated.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: (crying) I can’t believe I have to put up with this!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Cry me a river. I know you too well by now—you’re a tricky one. Well you’re not going to trick me, by God, so you can just cry until you piss yourself.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Traitor!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: What a show! I get it. You can turn off the spigots now; you’re making a mess.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: I’ll get you for this.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: By… by getting married, you pig.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You might as well beat yourself with your own shoe.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Oh, go away.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Fine by me.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: You’re going to leave just like that?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Yes, just like this, see? Walking.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Wait! I bet I know why you’re doing this.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I bet you don’t.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: You’re just jealous of Mireno.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Me, jealous of Mireno? Oh, that’s a good one! I’m proud to serve him, and his father Lauro, and to eat at their table. He’s a good, upstanding man, and for my part you’re welcome to him. But he’s a free spirit, and I don’t think he’ll be falling in love with anyone any time soon. His father brought him here as a baby, and you know what people say, that even though he walks around just like us, if you take off his rough cloak, like the bark off a tree, you’ll find some kind of nobility hidden underneath. There’s not a single shepherd in all of El Miño who doesn’t look up to him, or a girl who doesn’t sigh when he walks by, but Fortune seems to have made him as deaf to their sighs as Narcissus was to Echo. And now, since he’s ignoring you, you come running back to me. Well there’s no entrance here; this door is locked.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: You really don’t love me, do you?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: (crossing herself) Well I swear by God, I’ll make you pay.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You’ll make me pay?

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: That’s right, you’ll see soon enough. There’s nothing like a little rejection to change a man’s mind.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Well…

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Mark my words. There’s a certain shepherd I know of… When love goes astray, a shepherd will always bring it home again.

p.seg: I have to say, I’m a little nervous about what she might do. Anyone who isn’t afraid of her wouldn’t be afraid of the Devil himself!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Tarso! I’ve been looking for you all day.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Ah, Mireno! I’ve been having it out with Melisa for the last hour. The more she cried, the harder it was for me to keep from laughing. But what’s new?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Look, I know how much you care about me, which is why I’ve come to talk to you.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Whatever it is, you can tell me. Your father brought us up together, and even though I’m old enough to have a household of my own, you know I’d rather stay and serve in yours.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You don’t have to prove it to me, Tarso. You may be humble, but you’re a smart one. I’m about to toss my hope, like a javelin, as far as I can, and I want you to come with me and see if we can catch it. I’ve been down lately, filled with all these high and lofty thoughts, though I don’t know where I get them. It seems unfair that Fate made me a shepherd, when it could just as easily have made me a nobleman. I feel stuck, unable to rise above my miserable birth. I’m ashamed to say it, but sometimes I’ve even wondered if I’m actually Lauro’s son, or if maybe he took me from some nobleman’s house as a baby. I must have asked him a thousand times, when we’re alone, whether by any chance he used to have some higher station in life that he was cast down from, as it happens to so many people. I know we’re not from around here, and even though he dresses like a shepherd, he talks more like someone from the court. Every time I ask, though, he dashes my hopes, telling me all sorts of long stories that all end up at the same point: I’m nothing but the son of peasants. I know this should satisfy me, but it just makes me more anxious to get away and follow my guiding star—somehow I know it has good things in store for me. Besides, even if I was born poor, think how much more pride I could take in pulling myself up by my bootstraps. If you want to join me, Tarso, for better or worse, it’s up to you. I’ve made up my mind; now you make up yours.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: It’s enough for me to see you this excited—you’ve studied with the priest enough to know what you’re doing. I’m in! I do worry about your father, though.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: If I succeed, Tarso, I’ll make him forget all his troubles.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: When do you want to leave?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Now.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Today?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: This very minute!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: What about money?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I sold two oxen, and I’ve got the money right here. First thing, we’ll go straight to Avero, where we’ll find you a hat and a sword!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I just hope we don’t wind up running home like dogs with our tails between our legs!

div2.head: Scene 3
div2.stage: SETTING: Another part of the forest.
AT RISE: RUY steps out into the open, while VASCO stays back.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Sir, get back into the trees! I swear we won’t be here an hour before the posse catches us. Every last peasant in the neighborhood is after us like hounds after a hare, and when they catch us, they’ll crucify us. And we won’t be remembered, like Christ—we’ll be dismembered!

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: I’m afraid we’re not long for this world, Vasco. Even if we found a way to escape, we wouldn’t last for long on our own in the forest.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Steel is no match against the arms of hunger.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: I forged the Duke’s signature on a letter in order to avenge my sister, who was dishonored by don Duarte, and when that plan failed, I sought out someone to kill him for me. Still, the plans of the ill-fated always come to naught, and since I am such a one, let my life end now. It’s wrong to die of hunger when there is a sword at hand.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Is it really possible that someone who calls himself a man, like you, tried and true, would go to such great lengths to defend his sister’s honor? I mean, how do you know for sure she didn’t want the grapes picked from her vine?

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: Can you doubt it? Are there not thousands of cases in which—

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: (ad lib.) …I’m telling you, Melisa swore it to me…

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: I hear people coming.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: We’re lost!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: …It’ll be a pretty sight when she finds out I’ve skipped out on her!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You haven’t repaid her love very well.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Heavens, preserve us!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Hand her over to Pontius Pilate. She’s more fickle than a band of gypsies, and her love comes with more frills and flourishes than a song played on the organ.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Save us, Saint Anthony—blind them!

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: Calm down! It’s only two peasants, and they’re completely unarmed. They won’t do us any harm. Now, come on. (to MIRENO and TARSO) Where are you headed, my friends?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Good day, sirs! To town, to stock up on a few things. And you? This path leads away from the royal road to those huts at the foot of the mountain.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: My good shepherd, your words declare your kindness, so I’ll be frank. To avenge my sister’s dishonor, I tried to kill a powerful man, and now that the Duke has discovered my honorable plot, he has ordered his people to search this wilderness until they have captured me. Seeing no way out, I’ve taken the high road. (offering MIRENO his sword) My life, though honorable, has come to an end; now please, make it quick.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: What a sad tale! If the same miserable fate that made me a poor shepherd had given me more courage, I’d take up your cause myself. What we can do, if you’ll take my advice, is exchange clothes. Wearing these, you’ll be able to get away, and bide your time until your fortunes change, as I’m sure they will.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: May heaven reward you for this favor, since I cannot.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Let’s go into those trees and change our.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Does this mean I have to wear that get-up of yours? It has more bits and pieces than the innards on a butcher’s table.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: I’m afraid so.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Well, you’ll have to give me a lesson or two in how to put them on. They’ve got more entrances and exits than the city of Troy.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Let’s go, you’ll figure it out soon enough.

div2.stage: (They exit. DORISTO, LARISO and DENIO cross the stage, searching. MIRENO, RUY and VASCO enter, having exchanged costumes.)

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Where’s Tarso?

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Over there. He still can’t figure out how to untangle those breeches.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You should get going.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: Time will not erase the memory of this favor.

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: I’m a footman stuffed like a sausage into a shepherd’s casing.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: The purebred horse, left to its own devices, is content with the grass of the field and the hard iron bit. But the moment its owner places a gold-enameled harness on its head, it starts puffing and snorting and tearing up the grass, harness jingling wildly. In the same way I have grown up among the oak trees, speaking a rough tongue and wearing a rougher cloak. Yet as with the horse, this courtly dress has awakened my nobler thoughts, my pride increased by proud attire.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Would you look at these fabrications they’re making me wear? I can’t wrap my head around such highfalutin figaments . Look at all these crisscrossed streets and intersections. Have you ever seen so many slices, except on a melon? Is any astrologer’s chart this convoluted? It’s been an hour and I still can’t find a pocket.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: That’s enough, Tarso.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You shouldn’t be surprised: they’re clearly not the work of man.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Well, what else would they be?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Magic! These are worthy of Merlin himself—even the wisest men couldn’t make heads or tails of them. But anyway, now that I’ve been footmanified , and you’re a courtier, what do we do?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: We head for Avero. This outfit has lifted up my thoughts and I think we should aim even higher.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You may want to fly right up to heaven, but we’ll probably end up back down in the mud. Still, since you’re a new man now, and you might want to pass as a gentleman, shouldn’t you consider changing your name? Mireno doesn’t sound very lordly to me.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You’re right. I’m not a shepherd anymore, and Mireno no longer suits me. Don Dionís is a renowned and respected name throughout Portugal. From this day forward, that’s who I’ll be.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Not a bad choice. The kings we’ve had by that name have brought plenty of honor to it. Of course, you’ll need to give me a new name too, one that fits these new breeches of mine.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Choose one yourself.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Let’s see… I choose, I mean, if it’s all right with you…

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Brito Gómez. What do you think?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Perfect.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: That’s pretty good! We’re not even bishops, and we’ve given ourselves new confirmation names.

div2.stage: (DORISTO, LARISO and DENIO enter, with ropes.)

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: Unless they can fly, they got to be somewhere in this forest.

sp.speaker: DENIO
sp.p: Let’s look for ’em in the bushes.

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: Ain’t that them?

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Shhh! Where?

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: I swear, they look just like what we was told.

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: They ain’t got any weapons—tie ’em up.

sp.speaker: DENIO
sp.p: Surrender, sir!

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: Yield to the King!

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Yield to the Mayor!

div2.stage: (They catch MIRENO and TARSO from behind and tie them up.)

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: What’s going on?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: What… Why are you tying us up?

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Oho! You know how to be all smart when you’re plotting to murder the Count, and then you ask us why we’re tying you up?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: What Count? What murder? Do I even know you?

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: You’ll get your answers from the hangman, when he’s stringing you up like a fish by the guts, and by the gullet too.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: If I only had a sword, I’d make you regret this.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: It’s these clothes that have landed us in this mess. Is this the reward we get for our services, don Dionís ? What were you thinking?

sp.speaker: DENIO
sp.p: What are you yammering on about?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I don’t want to be Brito anymore, I want to be Tarso. I want to be a shepherd, not a footman. Take away these breeches and give me back my cloak. If I’m going to starve like the Hebrews in the desert, then send me back to be a slave in Egypt.

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Enough—let’s get going to Avero. We’ll get us a fine new gallows in the village for this!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Take heart, we’re going to Avero after all. When the Duke recognizes us for who we are, these goons will see how wrong they were.

div2.head: Scene 4
div2.stage: SETTING: A room in the DUKE’S palace.
AT RISE: JUANA is alone onstage. ANTONIO enters, in traveling clothes.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Antonio, cousin!

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Hush, don’t call me that! You must act as if you don’t know me, so the Duke won’t find out I’m in Avero. I’m on my way to Galicia on behalf of King Juan of Castile, but I simply had to make a detour here to see if rumor lies when it says that the Duke of Avero’s daughters are the most beautiful girls in all of Spain. As their lady in waiting, tell me, is it true?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: There are surely sights here to see and to admire, but you mustn’t be in such a hurry that you deny me entirely the pleasure of your company.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: My dear Juana, if the Duke recognizes me, he’ll oblige me to stay a while, and I’ll be in danger of falling out of favor with the King.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Well in that case, I suppose I’ll have to let you go. Still, if the Duke finds out that Antonio de Barcelo, the Count of Penela, has been in his house in secret, when he could have served you properly, he will be quite put out. No gentleman has ever visited without a royal welcome.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I know, I know—the Duke is of royal blood. But tell me, is his daughters’ beauty really what the world makes it out to be?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Do you ask out of curiosity, or has blind Cupid by any chance struck you with one of his arrows?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Cupid’s sparks can hardly make me love them when I haven’t yet had the pleasure of seeing them. Call it boyish curiosity that brings me to Avero.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I’m sorry to hear that. Our great nation is supposed to outdo all others where love is concerned, and since everyone knows Castilians fall in love at first sight, we Portuguese really ought to fall in love at first hearing. As for the Duke’s daughters, they deserve all the praise that comes their way. The older one, Madalena, would make Clytia jealous all over again—you remember, she was that nymph who was so jealous when the sun left her, she sat and watched him till she turned into a sunflower. It looks like she’s going to marry the Count of Vasconcelos. And then there’s Serafina, whose beauty is truly divine.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: And which of the two do you think is the most beautiful?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I’d have to lean toward the older one, though half the town would be quick to set me straight. There’s no point arguing over taste, and even less so over love; still, Avero is split into two camps, and both have a strong case.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Well, I must see them this afternoon, and then be on my way.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I can arrange things so their beauty might make a few stabs at your heart.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Serafina or Madalena?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Either—they’re both stunning. But look, here they come with the Duke. Let’s hide!

div2.stage: (They hide. The DUKE, COUNT, SERAFINA and MADALENA enter.)

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I tell you, don Duarte, everything will be done just so.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Since the King has consented that your eldest daughter shall be the wife of the Count of Vasconcelos, Your Grace may now write to him that, with his approval, the beautiful doña Serafina will be mine.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: I believe that he will favor this match as well.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Yes; however, let us not tell Serafina until we know for sure. She’s still just a girl and doesn’t yet know that her freedom will soon be captive to the yoke of matrimony.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: (to ANTONIO) See how soon your wish has come true? Now tell me, what do you think?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I don’t know which one my soul is more drawn to. Doña Madalena is beautiful, but Serafina is the very sun of Portugal. Through my eyes, my soul drinks flames of love mixed with snow from the crystal glass of her pale divinity. Rumor has come up short in her praise.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Come here, Madalena.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: She is a phoenix of beauty.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: (to MADALENA) This is very important.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: (to SERAFINA) Since the Duke gives me leave, my seraphic angel, I wish to speak to you, if there is courage enough in me that I may fly to a seraph’s height.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: My soul is helpless, watching love’s slow and steady assault. Yet even if it succumbs, I shall still feel myself victorious.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Cousin, I know you came here with your wits intact, but I’m afraid you may be leaving them behind.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: My daughter, the King does you a great honor. Consider how fortunate you are.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: My will is like wax. Your Grace may impress on it whatever seal most suits you, for my part must be only that of quiet obedience.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: A thousand times blessed is the father who hears such words.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: (to SERAFINA) You’ve raised my happiness to such heights, I’m afraid I may fall.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: I neither understand these philosophies, sir, nor are they to my taste.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: A seraph can easily grasp the heart and soul of such a matter. Do not say that you don’t understand, my seraph, what you know perfectly well.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: My Lord, how you talk!

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: I’m a man, what do you expect? God means us men to convey our intents with words, for if we were seraphs like you, we would speak with our thoughts alone.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Is love always so verbose?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Should it not be?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: I don’t trust boys or babblers, and Cupid would seem to be both.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Heaven, with a free hand, has made you perfect in every way.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: How pale! How discreet! Did you hear how shrewdly she answered don Duarte? Now he gets on my nerves. The heavens have enameled the gold of my love with jealousy.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: You don’t have much hope against a rival like him.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I’m still in need of a new secretary. Many have applied, but none seem capable of the position. It will cost me a great deal to be without one at a time like this.

div2.stage: (DORISTO, LARISO and DENIO enter, with MIRENO and TARSO in tow.)

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Make him go faster!

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: Look, there’s the Duke.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Herod give me patience.

sp.speaker: DENIO
sp.p: (to DORISTO) You’re the mayor; go talk to ‘em.

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Afternoon, old man. I’m the mayor, and, umm, you’re the Duke.

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: Closer!

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Well, you see, we knew, me and the blacksmith, and his wife, as how you wanted these scoundrels arrested, so we went: me, and Bras Llorente, and Gil Bragado… And then we talked with the constable, Pero Mínguez, and… (to LARISO) Don’t stand there like some dumb animal, come here and say the rest.

sp.speaker: LARISO
sp.p: I don’t want to. You say it.

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: I didn’t plan past this part. Well, in collusion, them two here is your thiefs, which me and Gil Mingollo caught, just so’s to serve you. And now, you should do what the village asks you to, Your Dukeness, and don’t forget what I said about that gallows.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What simplicity! I don’t know what they’re getting at, nor for what crime they have taken these poor men prisoner. Release them, and tell me yourselves what offense you have committed that they have brought you here like this.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: (kneeling) If it is an offense to have aided an unfortunate man chased and hunted by your people, and if you consider it brash to have swapped clothes with him in order to save his life, then I am guilty.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: You helped my secretary to escape? Yes, I see that you’re wearing his clothes. Tell me, traitor, why did you assist him?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Do not insult me, Your Grace, or call me by that name. I am not used to being treated with such contempt.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Who are you?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I am not yet—but I will be. In attempting to be more than I was born with, I have disdained that which I was and now look toward that which I am yet to be.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I have no idea what that means.

p.seg: What incredible boldness! He must have some strong stuff in him to be so fearless. I hate to see him in such straits.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Did you know the traitor whom you helped? You must have, to have put yourself at such great risk for his sake.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I knew that he wanted to kill a man who had dishonored his sister, and that you, who should have recognized his honorable intent, instead ordered his arrest. I helped him escape, appalled that you would pursue him while favoring the man who compromised his honor.

p.seg: What’s this? Has the secret of what I did to Leonela already been spilled?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Do you know who has disgraced this woman?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: If only I did, Your Grace. If I knew…

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: This was surely some trick of his to deceive you. You know where he is, and if you wish to go free, you will tell me.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Heaven forbid, even if I did know where he was, that a man like me should be frightened into committing such depravity!

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Is it depravity, then, to reveal a traitor? Lock him up. Unless he has lost his senses and his will to live, he’ll tell us where the man is hiding.

p.seg: I wish I could free him; a man of his demeanor doesn’t deserve such treatment.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: (to the COUNT) I fully intend to avenge you, sir.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Oh, he’ll talk.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I’d better get a healthy reward for all this!

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Let’s be on our way—I wish to reply to the King.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: A lot of good all these new clothes and names have done!

div2.stage: (LARISO and DENIO bustle TARSO and MIRENO offstage.)

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: (to DORISTO) Submit a request to my council for whatever you desire as a reward, and they shall pay you for your services.

sp.speaker: DORISTO
sp.p: Sir, in return for all what we’ve done, we want you to build us a nice new gallows, so’s we can hang the very finest men.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Serafina, I hate to see that man taken off like a common criminal.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Indeed, he has such a fine bearing, I’m tempted to intercede on his behalf.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You think he has a “fine bearing,” do you? That’s too bad; you wouldn’t be able to free him even if you tried.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: So you think.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Now, must you really go this afternoon?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Cousin! How could I, when I’m lost and blinded; when love, brave and cowardly love, has plundered my soul and will? If only to see her beauty one more time, I’ll stay the night.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Would you look at that! You truly are in love, aren’t you?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I fear, my dear, that Serafina’s spell will spell the end of all my life’s content.

div2.head: Scene 1

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Oh proud conceit, what foundationless towers have you erected in the air? Crazed imaginings, how dare you wander so free? Do you wish to expose my few failings to the judgment of gossips and wags? Yesterday the heavens could calm the rough sea of your hopes with ease, but now that very tranquility is disturbed by sleepless. nights. I said yes to the Count of Vasconcelos, or rather to my father in his name, but now a man has entered my heart through my eyes, and my honor, stunned, stood by and let him in. This would be a grievous fault, did I not know that love is a blind and senseless boy. Oh my heart, must you give yourself, in spite of me, to one both strange and a prisoner? Is it not just to love the Count? Ah, but love rides roughshod over the laws of reason. However, since, thanks to my insistence, my father has now set him free, I may begin to recover. He is a stranger, and once he goes, time and absence, those expert doctors of love, will quickly heal my disconcerted mind. But why do I propose so severe a remedy? If the wound may be healed, it is cruelty to remove the arm. Let us give love some room, then, since I do enjoy his presence. No one would deny a sick man a sip of water, even if his is a mere passing fever. I’ll call for him. (calling out) Doña Juana! Now restrain yourselves, you unbridled yearnings, lest you overwhelm me entirely. Do you wish to broadcast your affront? Shame conquers my mad desire, for, if it is madness to admit it in my soul, to speak it aloud is just as mad, and shameful too.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Don Dionís, that handsome young prisoner who has now, thanks to your help, been set free, wishes to speak to you.

p.seg: How quickly love takes the opportunity to bring itself into effect! I suppose that’s only prudent, since love itself is made of opportunities.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: He wishes to thank you for the favor you have done him.

p.seg: I sense asps hiding in the roses he sells.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Should I let him in?

p.seg: As a captive he captivated me; mistreated, he mistreated me; with his hands bound, he bound the hands of my affection. If he could kill while absent and a prisoner, what will he do free and in my presence?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Listen, tell him to wait. But no, he should go, it’s getting late.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Should he come back?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Didn’t I say he should? Now go.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: As you wish.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Wait—I don’t want him to complain.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Well, what should I say?

p.seg: …and to take me with him.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I suppose I’ll go.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Let him come to me; my Portuguese courage will carry the day. The wish to see with one’s own eyes is as natural a desire in an honorable woman as in a dishonorable one—the difference is that the first one keeps quiet about it. I’ll keep quiet then, and try to hide my disquiet, if a fire can be smothered without smoke. I’ll just take up the time with idle words. Oh, but if I close the door on the flames of love, they’ll just escape through the windows; if I close them up in my mouth, they’ll pour out my eyes. Still, no one will recognize them if I hold my tongue. As long as it is only my eyes talking, I will not invite any forwardness.

div2.stage: (MIRENO enters, dressed as a courtier, and kneels.)

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Although I have been forward in entering your presence, my lady, my wish is to thank you for the favor you have granted me, since the greatest sin is that of ingratitude. I was imprisoned for helping an unlucky man gain his freedom, but heaven has repaid me in the same coin, for thanks to your help, I am now free as well. But did I say free? I misspoke, for once a nobleman has received a favor, he is obliged, that is to say enslaved, to his benefactor. If only by becoming your slave I could repay my debt to you. Yet my humility is nothing compared to so many who come to offer you their necks, so let me do the same. So great is my debt, that only my life is great enough forfeit to make recompense.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Please, get up from the floor.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I would rather remain here, my lady.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Do as I say. (MIRENO rises.) Are you Portuguese?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I imagine so.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You imagine? Do you mean that you do not know who you are?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I believe I am Portuguese, though my father brought me to the village where he now lives when I was very young. He owns a small piece of land there, but his manner does him more credit than his station.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Are you of noble blood?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I believe so, judging by my natural demeanor, which is not that of the life to which I was born.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: And would your actions, were it necessary, prove your nobility?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I believe so. I have never shied from a noble act.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You answer “I believe so” to everything I ask. Do you think perchance I am interrogating you on articles of faith?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You may be, my lady, for my life’s faith is that of gratitude to your mercy. My faith is your desire.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Your gratitude is overwhelming.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I owe you my life.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Well then, now that you are free, what will you do?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I intend to go where I can achieve renown that exceeds my highest hopes.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: And where do you think you will be able to find such fortune?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: In war, where by force of arms I may attain the stature to which I aspire.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Would it not be safer to attain it in peace?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You could do so easily if you managed to have my father name you as his new secretary. As you know, the position remains vacant.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: My inclination was not born to serve, but aims rather higher.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Well if you wish to fly, feathers would certainly help.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: How am I supposed to fly with just the one feather of my pen?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: On the wings of favor. With the Duke’s confidence, you may achieve a thousand impossibilities.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: But confidence requires secrecy, and secrecy, they say, leads to fear.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Don Dionís, this is my will.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: It is your will that I serve the Duke? Well then, enough said. Let it be done as you wish, for with just one flight I have already risen to the highest heaven. If I may please you in this, I need not rise any higher. If the Duke will receive me, I will gladly be his secretary, since you, my lady, command it.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You see that I wish you to advance. Since I gave you your liberty, I would hate to see you lose it in war. I will make sure you are given the post, so that you will be able to stay here with us in this land.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Heaven is sure to remember your greatness.

p.seg: Honor, flee. My cowardly love is about to burst its bonds.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: What am I to think of this? Oh thoughts of mine, that float among the clouds, what do you make of all you’ve seen here? Declare yourselves, and tell me whether so much favor can arise simply from a noble inclination, or whether love may be at hand. Oh, what madness! It is foolish to even think such things, much less say them aloud. My humble state chastens my high-flying desire… but is it foolish to imagine that she who advances me harbors some secret love? Was I not set free by her hand? Did I not see her will through the windows of her eyes? Love’s got me now. Be still, mad tongue: it’s wrong to imagine that her favor comes from anything more than her natural nobility. But asking about my state and station, isn’t that love? Why would she care about such things—a woman’s curiosity? Yes, but would she say, “Don Dionís, this is my will,” like that, if she wasn’t in love? I know a peasant like me can hardly aspire to such heavenly beauty, but since when have I ever backed down from a challenge? I’ll wait and see, since time makes doubtful things certain.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: They’ve let us out of jail, like Daniel out of the lion’s den, and none too soon—I don’t have his patience. Still, I have a feeling that the worst is yet to come, just like the prophet Habakkuk said, so let’s get out of here! Or has Avero been so good to you, that you still dream about being a gentleman? Well, by God, we came pretty close to getting ourselves dubbed, but with a whip instead of a sword.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Brito, my friend!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I’m not Brito. I’m Tarso.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Listen, you idiot. I am now nothing less than secretary to the Duke of Avero.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: The lady who gave us our freedom continues to shower us with favors.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Well that’s different; now you’re really somebody.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Just wait till I tell you the details.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Congratulations! And now that you’re the great man, you can grant your faithful servant the small favor of getting me out of these breeches.

div2.head: Scene 2
div2.stage: SETTING: Another room in the palace.
AT RISE: ANTONIO and JUANA enter together.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Cousin, my love obliges me to stay, the King of Castile be damned. At this point I serve only one king, my desire. I’m a bird: blind to the snare, I alight on the branch of beauty and am caught. When I try to escape, I only get more tangled up. Don Duarte both serves and deserves doña Serafina, and I know that the Duke has promised to make her his wife, but I also know that if I leave now, I’ll be tortured by jealousy and doubt. If only my beloved seraph knew who I was, and showed me some sign of her favor, I could go with a light heart. Yet she knows nothing of me or of my great torment, and so my only relief is to stay. Whether I go now or later to the King doesn’t matter. My cousin, my lady, unless you wish me to waste away in exile from my beloved, do not ask me to leave Avero.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Antonio, as my cousin you know that I care about you. If I reproach you for staying, it’s only because in a town this size you’re sure to be noticed.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Never fear, I’ve found a way to do so safely and incognito. The Duke has never met me, and I happen to know that he is looking for an expert secretary.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I’ve a feeling I know where this is going.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Don’t you see that by entering the palace in that guise I can advance my hopes— given time, chance, and most importantly, your help?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: It’s an audacious plot, but rather beneath your position.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Any position is noble when it comes to love.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Well then, find a way.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I’ve already sent a note to the Duke asking him to give me the post.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: This is all very clever, but I do wish you had told me.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Prudence rewards. I’ve entrusted my note to Duke’s valet, who they say is one of his favorites.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: The Duke trusts him with everything.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Then I have much to hope for, as long as the valet remembers his promise.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Look, here comes the Duke.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: As I said, the position calls for one who conjoins nobility, discretion, and grace, not to mention a fine hand.

sp.speaker: FIGUEREDO
sp.p: I don’t know about his nobility, but I can assure Your Grace that in all other respects, no man in Portugal is better qualified to occupy the post than this one.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Enough. Since you praise him so, let me meet him.

sp.speaker: FIGUEREDO
sp.p: I’ll call for him at once—but here he is now, right before us. (to ANTONIO) Come forward, sir! My lord the Duke would like to meet you.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I place myself at Your Grace’s feet.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Rise. Where are you from?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I was born in Lisbon, sir.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: And whom have you served?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I was raised with don Antonio de Barcelo, the Count of Penela, and I bring with me letters of his, in which he favors my aspirations.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I care deeply for don Antonio, though we have never met. Why did you not give me these letters before?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I am not accustomed to obtaining through favors what I may obtain in my own right, and so I wanted meet you first, Your Grace.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: (to FIGUEREDO) I am impressed by his good form and style. (to ANTONIO) Very well, you are now my secretary. May your work prove your worth.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I submit myself, sir, to the proof of experience.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Doña Juana, what are Serafina and Madalena doing now?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: They were just in the garden together, though I understand that my lady doña Madalena is somewhat out of sorts.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What’s the matter?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: She’s been rather melancholy the last two days, but no one knows why.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I know what the problem is. She’s learned that I intend to give her a new state in life, and such changes are always the occasion for sorrow in a noble and honorable woman. It does not surprise me that she should fear a life of captivity. Now, look after this man. He comes from Lisbon and knows the Count of Penela, your cousin, so I’m sure you will have much to talk about.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Yes, my lord.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I am Your Grace’s most humble servant.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: A propitious start, I’d say.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: If that’s what you call toadying to your equal, then yes it was.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: At least I’ll be here, and there’s a chance I can quell my jealousy of don Duarte.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Oh, your beloved takes little notice of him. At the moment she’s spending all her time with her ladies in waiting, rehearsing for a play that she’s planning to perform for her sister to celebrate Carnival tomorrow.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Is she inclined to poetry, then?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: She simply loses her head over it. This afternoon she’s set on rehearsing the part with me alone in the garden, dressed as a man.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: And you tell me this just like that?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Why, how would you want me to tell you?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: How? By asking for my life, my mind, my very soul, in return for allowing me the wondrous chance to gaze on her in this manner. May you live more years than there are stars in the sky. May cruel time never consume the beauty you enjoy. May all your dreams come true, and the King of Portugal, madly in love with you, give you his hand, his scepter, and his life—

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Enough, before you lose your head and try to marry me off to the Pope! I’m happy to do this for you. Let’s go: I’ll hide you among the jasmines and myrtles that hedge the flowerbeds, and there, as long as you keep quiet, you can gaze to your heart’s content.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Say, is there a painter in Avero?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: The Duke employs some quite famous ones. Why do you ask?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I’d like to bring one to paint a portrait of my ravishing seraph. It would be easy enough for him to make a sketch while she’s dressing.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: And if doña Serafina notices, or the painter gives you away?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Money talks and money silences. Now, either stop holding me up or just kill me.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: You neither give me time to speak nor yourself time to listen, you rush me so. But very well, you’ll see how much I care for you. Now go find yourself a painter without a tongue, and be careful, or you may have to abort your plan. You lovers have such odd cravings, I’d swear you were pregnant.

div2.head: Scene 3
div2.stage: AT RISE: The DUKE and MADALENA enter together.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: If you wish to please me, my dear, you’re not doing very well; I’d rather die than see you upset. Fate has given you a husband to make you happy. Now go and reply to the letter his father the Duke of Braganza sent you, and don’t let me see any grief on your face, unless you wish to send me to an early grave.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: I’ll try not to be sad, sir, for your sake.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What you need is to find some distraction.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: I’ll try. And now, I would ask that you add one small favor to the many you have granted me.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Go ahead, on the condition that you forget all this sadness.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: The prisoner I asked you to free has now come to me for assistance, and I feel obliged to help him rise in your favor. He is a fine young man, and he has an excellent pen.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Tell me what he wants.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: He would like to take up the position of secretary.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: A short time ago I could have given it to him, but as of not a quarter of an hour ago the position has been filled.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: If it please Your Grace, I gave him my word, and now he expects some favor from me. Since you wish me to write to my fiancé and his father, and my hand at present is so poor, perhaps we could keep him here to teach me. It’s a great fault in a lady not to be able to respond when she receives a letter, or to respond in such a scrawling hand that it can’t be read. With lessons from him, I’d surely improve.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Well then, let him teach you to polish your drafts. Working will distract you from your sadness, which is born from the vice of idleness. He shall be your secretary.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Let me kiss your hands.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Sir, I come before you a very happy man.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Why is that?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: The King sends word that he approves my marriage to doña Serafina.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: That’s splendid news, my son. Still, you’d do well to give her some time to get used to the prospect. You know how heavily the idea of marriage weighs on her at present.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: My soul will endure these sufferings as proof of its devotion.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I’ll plead your case with her; you needn’t worry. The Count of Vasconcelos will be here shortly, and we’ll celebrate both weddings in good time. Cheer up, Madalena.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: I’ll be happy if it pleases you, sir. (The DUKE and COUNT exit.) They’re right in calling love both a sickness and a madness, since like a sick man, the lover always wants what’s worst for him. Honor, you’ve let into your house an adversary who will battle you for my very soul, and now I doubt his victory will be long in coming. Whoever seeks out danger shouldn’t be surprised when he stumbles over it. If Brutus’ wife Portia died from swallowing hot coals, what will become of me, if I must swallow the fire of my passions in silence? I’ll tell him, not with words, but with visible signs, the invisible torments that I suffer by not speaking.

div2.head: Scene 4
div2.stage: AT RISE: JUANA, ANTONIO, and a PAINTER enter together.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: This green myrtle here could be Cupid’s own hiding place; the jasmines and other shrubs will screen you like lattices.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: My seraph is an angel in this Paradise, but if she notices us, I’ll be Adam cast out of it.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I’ll make sure she rehearses the part right here, so that she’s in front of the painter and he can draw her more easily. She’s dressing herself as a man right now—an idea she’s quite taken with. I’ll go and tell her the garden is locked and empty.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: We’re both painters, you and I, but I already possess the portrait that enthralls and consumes me.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: I don’t understand.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: The mind is a canvas, or a tabula rasa as Aristotle calls it, on which may be painted a thousand different images.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: Well put.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Colors and shades are aspects of the object, which the eyes convey to the Common Sense. Here Estimation may admire them, but they appear only as rough sketches until Awareness illuminates and paints them with its own light. Once painted, Awareness puts them on sale, and presents them to the Will, that queen of infinitely good taste. She always loves what is fine, but her judgment is subject to what is presented to her. What she doesn’t know, she can never love.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: That is what the Philosopher says.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: She unrolls all the paintings and buys the one she likes, choosing better in some cases than in others. She puts this one in the frame of love and, charmed by the sight, hangs it in Memory, her most intimate chamber. In this same way, when I saw the uncommon beauty of my doña Serafina, I took up the paintbrush and began to paint. My Awareness completed the painting, and my Will bought it and placed it in my Memory. Finally, seeing how well it came out, the painter signed at the bottom, “ Amor me fecit ” – “Love made me.” Now do you see how the lover paints?

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: So, if you already have the portrait, what do you need me to paint her for?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: What I have is called a spiritual portrait. Sight is corporeal; thus, if I wish to gaze on her beauty in my solitude, I need you to paint me a corporeal portrait.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: There’s no philosophy like a lover’s.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I am a connoisseur in the ways of love. But listen, here comes my joy.

div2.stage: (They hide. SERAFINA enters, dressed in a man’s black tunic, accompanied by JUANA.)

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: You’re really going ahead with this? Aren’t you ashamed to see yourself like that?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Everyone dresses up for Carnival, so why can’t I? And you shouldn’t be surprised that I’m drawn to men’s garb, since I can’t be one.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: You look enough like one that I could fall in love with you. It’s going to be tonight, then?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I still wish you’d find some other way to entertain yourself, instead of acting.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: You cannot find another kind of entertainment that embraces so many diverse pleasures as the theater.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Oh, spare me.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What celebration or pastime is there that calls not for poetry? In the theater, may the eyes not delight in a thousand sights that banish their cares? Does music not beguile the ear and the mind delight in the conceit’s twists and turns? For the happy is there not laughter? For the sad, tears? For the sharp, wit? The fool and the simpleton, may they not learn? Is there not war for the brave, councils for the wise, and authority for the grave? There are Moors if you want Moors. If you prefer tournaments, you can have tournaments; if bulls, they’ll run bulls. Would you like to hear the epithets I’ve collected to describe the theater? It is a translation of life, sustenance for the discreet, a lady of understanding, a banquet for the senses, a bouquet of pleasures, a sphere of thought, an escape from the affronts of life, and a delicacy to match every purse, which starves fools but satisfies sages. Now which side would you rather be on?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I suppose I’ll side with the sages. I admit, I’m looking forward to this little farce.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I’m bewitched by the grace with which she speaks. Start drawing her at once. Oh, if only a mortal hand could capture from life the singular beauty of a seraph.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: She’s human—I can do it.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Doña Juana, bring me the mirror.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: If you look into it, my lady, beware you don’t fall in love with yourself.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Am I such a handsome man, then?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I’m afraid you’ll be another Narcissus.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Well! In that case, I’ll gather up my hair, so I won’t look like a woman even when I take my hat off. Why are you holding the mirror way over there?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: So that I can block the view of a painter who’s hidden in the garden.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What are you talking about?

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: By God, that woman’s giving us away! If the Duke finds out, we’re in for it.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: There’s a painter in the garden?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Yes, now let him do his work.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Good heavens! Has she gone mad?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Who would dare?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Cupid would, my dear, who—smitten with you—has hidden in the bushes to paint your portrait.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: That’s too true.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Let’s go over the part, now that I’m dressed for it.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: What’s this comedy called?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: The Cruel Lady of Portugal .

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: The poet must have had you in mind when he gave it that title.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What cruelty have you ever seen in me?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: To love no one.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: (putting on a cape and hat) Would it be fair that, to be kind to others, I should be cruel to myself?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Oh, take pity on the wretch condemned to hear such a thing!

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: Patience.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Enough, let me practice. It’s a superb role: a prince who challenges a count to a duel over a lady they both love. I don’t actually know what it means to be jealous, but watch and I’ll make believe I do.

lg.l: Oh Count, thy impudence is in th’extreme,
And of my patience passes o’er the bound.
I am surprised at thee, and Celia too:
At thee, that thou wouldst dare to speak to her;
At her, that she would hearken to thy words.
Moreover, since thou know’st th’advantages
That from my higher station couldst expect,
‘Twas pure contempt in thee, her to have loved,
And in her, to have lent thy love mad ear.
Hark now, and do not try to satisfy
My rage. All thy intents will be in vain
If, lacking arms with which to fight, seekest
To conquer me with words. Summon thy strength,
That my suspicions may be laid to rest.
For ‘tis not proper to be jealous of
So cowardly a man. Summon thy might,
Thou worm, thou vile enemy – now die!

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Careful! Your quarrel isn’t with me, my lady.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What do you think?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: You scared me. If you can act like that, what would you do if you really were jealous?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Have you ever seen such graceful jealousy?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Now watch. This time, reassured of my lady and her love, I will tenderly ask her forgiveness for frightening her.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Oh, that’ll be good. Go on.

lg.l: (acting) As heaven is my witness, reachèd not
My ire into my soul. Now, treasure dear,
Let us be friends, and quarrel not, for I
Myself do castigate. And let those eyes,
Those lovely maids, return to sport with me.
Remove that frown, my dears, for I would fain
Take you for peasants, hooded so. Wherefore
This cold disdain, my light, my star, my prize,
My solace, dearest treasure, and my peace?
Wilt not look on me? Art not satisfied?
Why, take this dagger, then, and kill me. Yet
Thou wilt not kill me, though thou may’st be wroth,
For ‘tis in me that all thy pleasure rests.
Now let this be the end, Celia my dear,
And do not make me cross.
I dare to hold
Thee so, for ‘tis but thee that I adore.
Now do not turn away from my embrace,
Nor hide from me the beauties of thy face.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: You’ve turned from ice to candle-wax. Now that’s the mark of a real Portuguese lover. Say, my lady, is it possible that someone who plays a lover so well can feel no love?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Fortunately, I’ve avoided that fate until now. It has so few advantages and causes so much pain. Now, listen to this part. You’ll see how well I can feign madness!

lg.l: Celia hath me forgot, and weds the Count?
Heavens! Woman and fickleness have got
The self-same root. What of the favors that,
Like flow’rs, the promise held of future fruit?
They were but almond blossoms, blasted now
By the north wind. Now I am mad, so may
Life end. Let life be lost, now sense is gone.
But let us to the wedding. Since we’ve paid
The cost, dear thoughts, let us be merry at
Our own expense. They’ll marry in the town
As peasants do, for love hath brought her low.
Then let us thither fly, oh jealousy,
Since thou hast wings of fire. We’ll soon arrive;
E’en here can we them spy. Here come the guests;
The drum keeps time for them to dance, and should
We not as well? Now: One two three, one two three …
Oh my desires, if Celia changed and did
Not keep in place, should you not dance as well?
Play on, old Pero Sastre, for the town
Will pay thee well enough. They’ve gone inside
To feast. And with this cloak of suff’ring now
I’ll cover myself o’er, and sit unseen
In this dull corner, as is my desert.
And now they pass out hazelnuts to all,
And toasted chickpeas. Ho, there! Here, you fools!
I’ll take a handful.
—Me, a fool? Thou liest!
I lie? Take that!
—Wouldst slap me? Die, thou knave!
Take that! What’s this?
— ‘Twas nothing.
—Let’s be friends.
I’d like to be.
—Now here comes old sir priest:
May many a good year this house rejoice
With weddings.
—Father, here’s a seat for you.
Oh, no.
—Here, take this chair.
—No, I could not.
But I insist.
—This bench is fine, still, I
Won’t make thee beg.
—The old man’s at his ease.
Hernán Alonso, give the priest some wine;
Now let him drink.
—But oh, it tastes of brine.
So beauteous Celia tastes of jealousy.
And now at last the time for vows is come:
The guests are on their feet, the pair in front,
The priest there in the middle.
—Fabio, dost
Thou take the beauteous Celia as thy wife?
I do.
—And Celia, dost thou Fabio take?
As husband and as master.
—Oh, you dogs!
And in my presence! Hold, I am the prince.
Death to the bride and groom, the priest, the guests
And the whole town.
—Oh, he is killing us!
Burn them, oh jealousy, with your wild flames.
Samson am I; among the Philistines
Come I to die. These flames none may withstand,
Kindled by love and by suspicion fanned.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Good heavens, get a hold of yourself! I’m not Celia, or Celio.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: I forgot myself. Now, let’s go. I’ll put my dress on over this until it’s time.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: That was wonderful. Your gloomy sister is sure to enjoy herself tonight.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: They’ve gone.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Leaving me blinded and sad.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: Now, you really want me to paint her as a man?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Yes, it will be a memento of what we’ve just seen. But change the suit.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: You don’t want it to be black?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: It would dress my hope in mourning. Better that it have the color of fresh pastures, flecked with gold. Gold for my love, and green for my envy.

sp.speaker: PAINTER
sp.p: As you wish.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Money is no object. It’s not out of stinginess that Cupid goes naked.

div2.head: Scene 5
div2.stage: AT RISE: MADALENA and MIRENO enter together.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Starting today, you will be my writing tutor.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: What have you seen in me, my lady, that you would ennoble me this way? Surely the student will teach the master.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Don Dionís, since my love is so great… for the Count of Vasconcelos, I would like, before he arrives, not only to have good handwriting, but to be able to write to him with words that express the deepest stirrings of my heart. I am inexperienced in the art of love, and so you must instruct me how to declare what I feel in my soul, as love commands. My love is boundless, but my words fall short. You seem to be a man of many skills, and so you must teach me both to write, and to declare my love to the Count.

p.seg: So it wasn’t for my sake, but to serve as a go-between for her and the Count? You see, foolish love, how groundless were the fantastical towers you built, and how they’ve come crashing down? I’m like the mule who bore the holy image on its back for the festival. When the people bowed, the reckless beast thought it was to him. Impatiently, he tried to throw the image off his back, until they flogged him back into place, and he realized his foolish mistake. So, this is how she favors my recklessness? Enough. It’s clear that I’m the ass; the holy image is the Count.
I had to shock him that way. It would have been too much to speak openly.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: At your service.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You’re unhappy.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Me?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: What is it?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Nothing.

div2.stage: (MADALENA trips; MIRENO gives her his hand.)

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Oh, dear! I stumbled… My shoe turned.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: My lady, are you hurt?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: I don’t believe so.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Was it forward of me to take your hand?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You should know, for the courtier, a proffered hand is a step toward many things.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: (reading) “A proffered hand is a step toward many things!” What could that mean? Tell me, vain thoughts, am I losing or winning? What confusion, what suspicion is this? Tell me, for heaven’s sake, is this not love? Or am I just the ass bearing the image of the Count of Vasconcelos. What are these better things toward which, with her hand, I might step? If she only loves the Count, what can I possibly hope for? What do I know? Tell me, hand or foot, why must you keep me up at night? Confusion, love, suspicion: am I loved? Or am I just the ass bearing the image of the Count? Her proffered hand can only mean that I must lend a hand to the passion the Count and her love inspire in her. Oh shame, suffer in silence. No more bold flights—it was folly that lifted my soaring ambition to the stars. I’m just the ass bearing the image of the Count.

div2.head: Scene 1
div2.stage: SETTING: Lauro’s house, a shepherd’s hut.
AT RISE: LAURO enters, leaning on RUY, who is dressed as a shepherd.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: It’s no use. Children inherit the misfortunes of their fathers, and in this case it’s the only inheritance he’s got. He was the only support of my old age.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: Come now, your age must have taught you more prudence than that. If anyone has a right to lament his fate, it’s me. Heaven has taken away my honor, my country, my land and my name. You’ve lost a single son, and you still have good reason to hope that he’ll return.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: You wouldn’t say that if you knew the sorrows I’ve lived with all these years. I’m not from this rough country, Ruy, and these rough clothes you see me in are not my true inheritance. My name isn’t Lauro, and these mountains are not my home. In fact, my noble blood has never known how to cultivate the earth. They call me don Pedro of Portugal, and I descend in a direct line from the Portuguese kings. King Duarte was my brother, and the man who reigns now is my nephew.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: By God, you’re the Duke of Coimbra! Let me kiss your feet.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Never mind that. My brother, the King, died in his youth, leaving behind a six year-old son and naming the Queen and myself as regents. In time the Queen died, the prince came of age, and a thousand flatterers soon surrounded the throne, slamming the palace doors in the face of truth. They persuaded the young King that I had poisoned his mother, and showed him forged letters claiming that now I was plotting to overthrow him. He believed them, and ordered that I be stripped of my estate, and all the wealth I’d earned as regent. I was taken to a fortress where, in spite of all the tears and supplications of Isabel, the daughter I had foolishly given him as his wife, he ordered them to cut off my head. That very night, I made a rope of my bed-sheets and escaped over the wall, sending word for my wife to follow. We took cover in these mountains, where she soon died in childbirth. She left me a handsome son, though, who has grown up wearing those rustic rags, dealing in sheep and pastures, turned from a duke into a shepherd. Twenty springtimes have passed, bringing flowers in May and new flourishing to the grass and to my heartache, and still I remain as you see me here. All that would be nothing, though, had I not lost the son who could make me forget all my troubles. Now tell me that I don’t have good reason to miss the sight of him in my miserable old age.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: Yours is yet another of the many tragedies from the capricious pen of Time that are played out on the world’s stage. Your Grace’s troubles have made me forget my own. But I saw clear signs of hope in your son’s presence: like coals over a banked fire, his cloak concealed the flame of his nobility. May both he and your good fortune soon return to you.

div2.head: Scene 2
div2.stage: SETTING: A room in the palace.
AT RISE: MIRENO and TARSO enter together.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: You want more proof than what she said: “for the courtier, a proffered hand is a step toward many things”? Could a noble lady like her spell it out any more plainly? You’re the most timid, clammed up lover I ever saw. What are you waiting for—for her to play the man’s part? In what species of animal is the female not celebrated, wooed, and pursued with all sorts of loving signs? You have to start the courtship; anything else would break the natural order of things. Talk to her. Don’t lose a woman of her quality to shyness.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Tarso, all my doubts and fears are like a twisting labyrinth. Could the heavens possibly prefer me to the Count of Vasconcelos? When I compare myself to him, I see that he is a man of rank, a cultivated gentleman, and heir to the Duke of Braganza. I, on the other hand, am a humble shepherd, the lowly branch of a poor trunk. A noble woman like her couldn’t possibly prefer copper to gold. And yet look at all the ways she’s favored me: engaging me in friendly conversation, pausing and gazing, the riddles and roundabout ways she reveals her desires, pretending to stumble (if she was pretending), giving me her hand… All these things only encourage me. I’m on fire, Brito, caught between hope and fear, so that when I’m about to speak my mind, I can’t bring myself to do it. Fear holds me back, love pushes me on, and when I finally work up the courage to say something, shame creeps up and gags me.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Shame? And you call yourself a man? Look at this baby, this damsel in distress. There’s no room in the palace for a shy courtier. If Cupid had any shame, they wouldn’t paint him naked. Don’t be afraid that you’ll offend her. Love may be blindfolded, but his mouth is perfectly free. Speak up, or I’ll do it for you. If you don’t, your step toward many things you may turn out to be a step to nowhere.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Brito, I know that a mute love makes no sense, but in speaking I risk losing what I possess in silence. Now at least I can imagine she loves me, and my vague, crazy hopes live on. If by declaring my love I face disappointment and reproach, isn’t it wiser to hold my tongue and enjoy a doubtful love rather than a certain disdain?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: A wise man once said there are three places shame and fear never belong: in the pulpit, in the palace, and in love. You’re here at court and Fortune has cut a wide path for you. Don’t turn back now.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: But she tells me she loves the Count of Vasconcelos.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: A roundabout way of testing your love. Try talking to her. Because, by God, if you lose her, we might as well pick up our pitchforks and head home.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Don Dionís, my lady calls for you.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Coming.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Now’s your chance: open your heart, sir… and remember to speak slowly.

div2.head: Scene 3

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Cupid, little boy, why so fearful and shy? When did you grow up and come to know shame? Is it possible that you live in don Dionís, and that he calls you his god? If so, if he loves me, why won’t he say so? Silence is a great fault in a man; he really ought to unburden himself. Just once, let his tongue tell me what his eyes express all too well. If his humble station holds him back, my bold liberties should have allayed any doubts. My eyes declare in vain that I adore him. By giving him my hand, at the expense of all propriety, I paved the way as far as my honor would allow. Blind boy, in giving me a lover, did you have to make him mute? But I shouldn’t wonder at it, for love has humbled me as well. I could spell it out plainly, and he still might not believe.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Don Dionís is here for your lesson, my lady.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: A lesson in silence, since it would seem he has no words. I can’t bear this silence any longer. I’ll declare my love openly, against all common sense and practice, but I’ll do it so that, in telling him everything, I leave him even more confused.

div2.stage: (She sits in a chair and pretends to be asleep. MIRENO enters.)

p.seg: My heart is thumping. She’s quiet; she must not have seen me. She’s just sitting there, with her hand on her cheek. Why doesn’t she answer? Oh, she’s asleep. Take heart: now’s the time to go look at the beauty that clouds my mind. Her eyes are closed; I can approach without fear, since she can’t wound me with her arrows of love. Did the Author of nature ever make a more perfect beauty? If I could only kiss her hand. Should I? Yes. But no, it’s a divine relic, and my humble mouth is unworthy to touch it. I may be a man, but I’m shaking! What is this? Courage. She is sleeping, isn’t she?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: (as if dreaming) Don Dionís…

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Did she call my name? Yes, she must be waking up. Imagine if I’d gone through with my plan! But is she awake? No, I think she may be dreaming. And dreaming about me, no less. If she calls my name while she’s asleep, surely she can’t despise me when she’s awake. Oh God, if only I knew what she were dreaming!

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Don’t go away, don Dionís. Come here.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Her dream calls me to come. What luck! It’s only right for me to obey, since, even asleep, she is my master-mistress. Speak up, love, and don’t be shy.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Don Dionís, now that you’ve come to teach me both to write to and to love the Count of Vasconcelos…

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: …let us find out whether you know what love is, and what is jealousy. It would be a grave misfortune if I remained in the dark, and you can’t very well teach what you don’t know. Tell me, are you in love? Why are you blushing? What are you ashamed of? Answer me; don’t be afraid. Love is a natural tribute and a debt in all living things, from the angel to the brute. Since that is so, why are you so shy?

div2.stage: (She questions and answers, still as if asleep.)

sp.p: Now, are you in love? – Yes, my lady. – Thank God I can get at least one word out of you!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Could there be a lovelier dream? I must be the luckiest man in the world! Though I’m more inclined to believe I’m the dreamer here, since I’m surely not awake.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Have you told your lady of your love? – I have not dared to. – So, she knows nothing? – She must have seen the flames of love in my infatuated eyes, which cry out in silence. – The mouth should perform that task; the eyes speak an unknown tongue. Has she not given you occasion to declare yourself? – So much so, that my shyness amazes me. – Speak, then. Delay can only hurt your love. – I’m afraid to lose by speaking what I enjoy by keeping quiet. – That’s just foolish. A wise man once compared a mute lover to a Flemish painting that’s always kept rolled up: the painter won’t get very far if he never shows his paintings to the public he wishes to buy them. The court is no place for reticence. Unroll your painting so that it may be sold. The ill that’s kept hidden is the most difficult to cure. – Yes, my lady. But the inequality between us holds me back. – Is love not a god? – Yes, my lady. – Well then, speak, for his laws are absolute, toppling the mightiest monarchs and leveling crowns and clogs. Tell me who you love, and I’ll intercede for you. – I don’t dare. – Why not? Am I not fit to be your messenger? – No, but I’m afraid. Oh… – What if I say her name? Would you tell me if she is, by any chance, me? – My lady, yes. – Let me finish! And you are jealous of the Count of Vasconcelos, right? – It’s hopeless. He is your equal, and the heir of Braganza. –Equality and likeness don’t come down to whether a lover is noble, humble or poor, but to an affinity of soul and will. Make yourself clear from now on, don Dionís, I urge you. When it comes to games of love, it is better to overshoot than to fall short of the mark. For some time now I’ve preferred you to the Count of Vasconcelos.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: (crying out) Oh merciful heavens, what am I hearing?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: (as if waking) Good Lord, who’s here? Who let you in, don Dionís?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: My lady…

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: What are you doing here?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I came to give you your lesson, my lady, but I found you asleep, so I waited here until you woke up.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: (rising) I must have drifted off.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: If you always dream like you did just now, my lady, I am a fortunate man.

p.seg: Thank God the man finally said something!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: It wasn’t hard to figure out.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Are you another Joseph, then?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: No, I’m no interpreter. I can only summarize.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Then tell me how you know what I dreamed.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You spoke aloud in your sleep, my lady.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
