sp.p: God help me! I don’t remember anything. Tell me what you heard.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I don’t dare.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: It must have been very bad, if you can’t bring yourself to tell me.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Nothing worse than being in my favor.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: But I must know. On my life, just tell me.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: That’s quite an oath. It encourages me to be bold. My lady, while you slept… I can’t.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Enough, don Dionís; this is becoming tedious.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You showed openly that you favor me.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: I did? How?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You recognized my jealousy, and in dreams you promised me…

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: …that you prefer me to the Count of Vasconcelos. You see, I realize the import of this—

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You should not believe in dreams, don Dionís, for dreams are dreams, and nothing more.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Now where did that come from? Just when my I get my hopes up, she piles disdain on the other side of the scale, and the needle is stuck at zero. I should just give up speaking once and for all. Just my luck, that she who loves me in her dreams should hate me when she wakes. Let my soul now temper its passion, serve better masters, and never trust dreams again, for dreams are dreams, and nothing more.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Well, how did it go?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: How do I know? It’s as if she loves me and hates me in equal measure. I’m better off going back to my old shame and modesty.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: So, in other words, you did about as well as the three guys with only one shoe…

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Tell me about it some other time. Oh Brito, I miss how simple life was back in the village. Here everything is full of confusion and deceit. I think it’s time to write to my father and tell him how things are going, if I can find a way to do it in secret.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I don’t want them to know who I really am here till I see where this whole intrigue ends.

div2.head: Scene 4
div2.stage: AT RISE: SERAFINA and ANTONIO enter together.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Don Antonio, if that is who you really are, your presumption is shocking. To enter my father’s service under false pretenses, to deceive me and insult him, does not befit a gentleman. Did you somehow imagine you had only to disclose your identity and I would simply give in to your pleasure?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I stopped here to see my cousin and Cupid did the rest.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: My father has given his word to don Duarte that I am to be his wife, but even if he hadn’t, or if I weren’t inclined to obey, I'd marry him to punish your madness. Leave Avero this instant, or I’ll call for my fiancé to deal with you.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Am I worthy of such contempt?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Leave, sir, or I shall scream.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Let me explain.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: By God, if you haven’t left town within the hour, I’ll marry don Duarte this very night out of spite. The sight of you is an affliction. Now, sir, leave.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: You viper, you hide your venom in the roses of your beauty. Can you really disdain my amorous sighs? This is torture! Very well: since you exile me from the paradise of your presence, may love make you another Narcissus, to cry, like me, without consolation. If I’m to be banished from the sight of your beauty, my only recourse is to banish this image from my breast. (He takes out the portrait.) Erase, my soul, the portrait love painted for you, as I cast down this spiteful one here. (He throws it on the floor.) Farewell, cruel portrait of a stone. Time, that wise doctor, will heal me of my ills. Meanwhile, it is fitting that you lie on this floor, stone-cold and hard as you are. Stay, fire, and burn here in the snow.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What madness love causes! Good thing I’ve never put myself under the yoke of that harsh tyrant. What’s that he threw on the floor, calling it spiteful and every other sort of name? (She picks it up.) A portrait! It’s of a man, but to me he looks… like I look. Indeed, like me exactly. It’s like glimpsing my own reflection. Who could this be? It doesn’t look at all like don Antonio. And why did he throw it at my feet? Could there be a man who looks so much like me? No; and even if there were, what could he possibly have done to make don Antonio hate him so much? There’s a riddle wrapped in an enigma here. Here comes doña Juana. She’s his cousin, she must know. (JUANA enters.) Doña Juana, would you look at this portrait? Have you ever seen such a resemblance in your life?

p.seg: This must be the portrait that painter made. Heaven help me if she finds out I let them into the garden.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Isn’t it remarkable?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Oh yes, indeed, remarkable.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Your cousin, in a fit of pique because I don’t love him, threw it on the floor and then stormed out like a madman. I looked to see what it was, and found the resemblance unsettling. You have the keys to his heart; how do you explain this?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: My lady, I’m as ignorant as I am astonished by it.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: All the worse for me. I’d give anything to know who it is.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Well, in that case…

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: If I go tell Antonio you’ve decided to grant him some favor, he’ll come running back in an instant.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Clever! But he’s probably already gone.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: I doubt it. I’ll find him.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Hurry!

p.seg: It’s a cosmic punishment for the woman who thought she was above love to fall for her own portrait!

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: It wasn’t in vain that don Antonio cast you down here; you’ve managed to win my heart where many living men have failed. Indeed, if the original is as handsome as you make him out to be, I certainly wouldn’t push him away. Don’t be flattered; it’s no surprise I’ve had such a sudden change of heart. As they say, birds of a feather…

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: (to ANTONIO) Careful how you answer.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: (to JUANA) A little white lie will do the trick.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Don Antonio.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: My lady.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: You’re a short-tempered man.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: It comes of being Portuguese. But how could I have retained my composure, when you ordered me to leave within the hour?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: You misunderstand the ways of women. A woman’s anger, sir, is like a French horse: wild at first, but quick to spend itself. Time heals all wounds. Now, since you’ve calmed down as well, would you tell me why you threw this at my feet? Whose portrait is it?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: (to JUANA) Don’t believe a word of this. (to SERAFINA) I wish I could tell you the truth, my lady, but I do not dare.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I fear a terrible punishment.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: You have nothing to fear, I assure you.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Your presence gives me the courage to speak. To die for the sake of a friend would be a small sacrifice.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Go on.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I’m sure, my lady, that you know the long, sad story of the Duke of Coimbra, who governed this kingdom so well in both war and peace. He was from the same royal lineage as your father, so I’m sure you’ve both wept over his misfortunes.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: I overheard my father tell my sister one day, and it has troubled me ever since. They say it’s been twenty years since envy banished him from Portugal, along with his wife and their tender young son. I’d love to know if he’s still alive, and where he’s living.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I’m afraid the Duchess has died, but her memory lives on in her husband and unhappy son. My father was their kinsman and friend, and when they escape from prison, he risked life and limb to offer them help. He has kept them hidden on one of his farms, where, wearing rough cloaks, the two have tilled the land, watering it with their tears and harvesting only thorns in return. The son, to whom heaven granted a generous share of discretion, courage and charm, was my childhood companion. He’s like the other half of my soul; the knot of friendship has made our lives one. As it happens, about six months ago he passed through Avero, and on seeing you his heart was stolen right through his eyes. Since then, the whole valley has been echoing with the declaration that Serafina is the culprit. A thousand times he’s been determined to tell you of his misfortunes, but fear has held him back, knowing that the King has proclaimed his family to be traitors. I feel the unending tears he cries as my own, and so I promised him to tell you of his love, and to bring his portrait for you to see. When I arrived and heard how disdainful you were, and how little inclined to the bridle of love, I didn’t dare say anything about him until I could speak to you privately. That’s why I persuaded my cousin to find me a position with the Duke. I soon learned that he wanted to marry you to don Duarte, and so, to head that off, I showed you the flames of my feigned love. When you rejected me with such fury, I left behind the portrait, knowing that its beauty would soothe your heart and temper your arrogant vanity. In short, beautiful Serafina, the owner of this portrait is don Dionís of Coimbra.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Don Antonio, is this true?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: So true that, if he were here and knew that you loved him, I believe he would lay his soul at your feet, even at risk to his life.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: If that’s really so, I’m not sure there’s room in my heart for don Duarte. By God, this is the son of that poor duke, don Pedro! Could I see him?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: This very night. If you agree to bring his woes to an end and speak to him in the garden, he’ll be waiting.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: It would be rank ingratitude to fail to love so noble a man, equal to my rank, who returns my love. You have been discreet in all of this. I trust you to keep my secret, and arrange it so that we may speak. Now farewell.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: You’re going?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: I’ve already said too much.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Is it true that don Pedro and his son are still alive?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Hush; I only said that to buy some time. I don’t know anything about the Duke, or where he took his wife and his son. I’ll be don Dionís by night, and Antonio by day, and that way, with a little help from Cupid, my hard work will pay off.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Just be careful.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Love has ordained my happiness under another name; my own is worth nothing to me now.

div2.head: Scene 5
div2.stage: AT RISE: The DUKE and MADALENA enter together.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: I’d like to see you at your lesson. I saw the address on the envelope of the letter you wrote to the Count of Vasconcelos yesterday, and I was impressed. You’re writing very clearly now.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Apparently it’s still not clear enough for my teacher don Dionís to understand.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Did you call, my lady?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Yes. My lord the Duke would like to see how I’m improving. You’ve seen how much better I write, right?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Yes, my lady.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Why, not a quarter of an hour ago, I wrote out a letter half asleep that was so clear, even someone who couldn’t read would understand it. Do I make myself understood, don Dionís?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Quite.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Perhaps you could come up with some words to say in its favor.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: My silence is praise itself; the only fault I find is in the last line. There may have been something amiss with the pen, but it’s very hard to read.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You mean the blot at the end.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Well… yes.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: I made it on purpose.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I’m afraid it obscured everything around it.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: A little blot is hardly a big problem. Surely you could have corrected it?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Carve me a quill.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I’ll do so in short order, my lady.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Get on with it. For all your words, when it comes to action you always seem to come up short.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Really, I’m quite satisfied with your writing.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: It’s pointless; he’s deaf to all the pointers I give him. Oh, hand it over.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Madalena, contain yourself.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Would you like the point carved short?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Don’t be short with me. I want it long. Now carve it that way, or don’t bother.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: It will be ready shortly, my lady.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: You’re being awfully rude!

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Shy men are nothing short of infuriating.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Here, in short, is your pen.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Let’s see. Good God, it’s awful!

div2.stage: (She throws the quill on the floor.)

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What did you do that for?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: You’re always giving them to me with hair on the point. Use that knife properly for once, and clean it off. I’m not sure what to make of you, always leaving hair on the quill so I can’t write clearly even if I try.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Your Grace, I bring word from the Count of Vasconcelos. He is only a day’s journey away.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: His leave from the King is so brief, however, he’ll have to be married and return immediately. If Your Grace will make the necessary preparations, I’ll go now to meet him.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Did he not write me?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: He sent this note.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: My daughter, the moment we’ve been awaiting has arrived. Set this aside and make ready: you’ll be married tomorrow.

div2.stage: (The DUKE and COUNT exit; Madalena starts to write.)

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Don Dionís, read this note once I have finished it, and follow my instructions.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: If I’ve lost my chance, what’s the point?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Love is nothing but chance.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: (reading) “Time is short. This night in the garden will see an end to the fears of the shy courtier.” Tonight? What luck! Am I dreaming? Am I mad? It can’t be. “…in the garden…” My God, it’s written right here! I have to find Brito. Could there be a happier ending? The Count of Vasconcelos will be the jealous one tonight.

div2.head: Scene 6
div2.stage: AT RISE: LAURO, RUY, MELISA and VASCO enter together, the men reading a letter.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: This is wonderful news! Can it be true? My son is a courtier in Avero? How times change. But what am I waiting for? Let’s go see them—

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: And what if they recognize me?

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Blacken your face like a coalminer. I’ll have a good day tomorrow in Avero, even in my old age. I feel alive again. (to MELISA and VASCO) You stay here and look after the house.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Vasco, what about Tarso? Doesn’t he ask about me?

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: It seems to me he doesn’t give a damn about you. And he’s not Tarso anymore, either.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Who is he?

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Brito.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Cruel Tarso, my enemy, my tyrant. Devil take the house; I’ve got to go and put some sense into you.

div2.head: Scene 7
div2.stage: SETTING: The palace garden at night.
AT RISE: SERAFINA and JUANA are at the window.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Doña Juana, my honor is on the line. But if I delay, the Duke will marry me off tomorrow.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Don’t be afraid, my lady. My cousin’s gone for him, and they’ll be here any minute.

p.seg: Cupid, tonight your mystical powers have made me both a false don Dionís and a real don Antonio. I’ll have to speak for both of them. I see people in the window.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: I hear something—my hope wasn’t in vain. Hello there, is that don Antonio?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Yes, my lady.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Is don Dionís with you?

p.seg: Don Dionís? That’s a good one. But wait, is that doña Madalena? Mireno told me to watch out for people here, but it looks like someone’s already come to take his place. Unless it really is don Dionís?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I bring with me a don Dionís whose soul you already own, but who comes to lay the rest of himself at your feet. Now speak, my friend. What are you waiting for? (changing his voice to become don Dionís) Can’t you see I’m speechless, contemplating such glories? To pay the great debt I owe you, my lady, with words would be a disgrace, and so I do not dare to try, but rather rein in my tongue. Love is a god, and will surely pay my debt for me.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: That’s quite a voice he’s got.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Can you not pay me on credit, sir?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: (as don Dionís) I can certainly offer you a good backer. Don Antonio will give me credit, won’t you? (as himself) Most assuredly.

p.seg: By the devil, it’s only one man, but he sounds like two.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: (as don Dionís) I am in great danger speaking to you here. I beg you, make my happiness certain and bring my pains to an end.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: What would you have me do?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Remember, my lady, that if you wait till daybreak you’ll have no choice but to marry don Duarte. You can’t afford to wait.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Oh dear!

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: A fine time for cold feet. Do we let him in?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Do as you wish.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: (alternating voices) Don Dionís, love has brought you the greatest of good fortune. Use it well. – I’m your friend for life! – And I your slave. Now go on; I’ll wait for you here. –Farewell, don Antonio.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Has he come in?

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: So this is how love brings us down! Well, at least it’s not the love of don Duarte; that’s something. If only my father can forgive me.

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: It’s time, dear.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: There’s something fishy going on here. A don Antonio who talks to himself, says he’s going to stay put, and then walks right in. I’ll bet that was the devil himself!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: He must have fallen asleep, as usual.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Mireno, someone’s been here and taken your place!

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You idiot, what are you talking about? I sent you to see if there were people, and you’ve just been dawdling here!

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: There were people.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: One don Antonio, and one don Dionís—two people who were really one.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Are you out of your mind?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I’m telling you, by God, some trilingual scholar just waltzed in to meet your doña Madalena, and either he can be in two places at once, or he’s your ghost. I swear, he was craftier than twenty Ulysses. Unless I dreamed this whole thing, you’re not the first don Dionís trying to get in there tonight.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: You must have dreamed it.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: If you say so. (MADALENA comes to the window.) There’s someone in the window.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Oh dear, I hear people! Hello there, is that don Dionís?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: To my great fortune, my lady.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Come in, my shy one.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Now do you believe that you dreamed it?

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Oh, I don’t know.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: If my shyness was a shame, then farewell to shame.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: I can’t figure it out; I definitely saw two don Dionises go into that house. This whole place must be bewitched!

div2.head: Scene 8
div2.stage: SETTING: The palace garden, the next morning.
AT RISE: LAURO and RUY enter together.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Well, Ruy, here we are in Avero.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: I was a great man here not long ago, and now I return as a poor shepherd.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: How times change! And what a splendid palace the Duke has now. When I—

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: A drum-roll this early in the morning?

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: What could that be about?

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Vasco, watch out! Our masters are right over there; we can’t let them see us.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: Look, the Duke! Something big must be happening.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: It looks like he’s going to issue a proclamation.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Don Duarte, no other news could make me happier. My cousin don Pedro’s troubles are through, provided he’s alive.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Good heavens, what am I hearing? Am I the cousin he means? It can’t be.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Before you go to meet your brother-to-be, I want you to hear what the King has decreed. (to FIGUEREDO) Read the proclamation.

sp.speaker: FIGUEREDO
sp.p: (reading) “Our lord King Alfonso the Fifth commands that the inI’d like to congratulate you, sir, through my tears.nocence of don Pedro of Coimbra, and the treason of his accuser, Gabriel Fernández, be solemnly proclaimed throughout his royal domains. The King reinvests his noble vassal don Pedro with all his estates. Wherever he resides, if he be alive, he is to be treated with the respect due to the King himself. Furthermore, the King names don Pedro’s sons as heirs to the ducal estate, and declares Gabriel Fernández and his sons traitors in perpetuity, commanding that salt be scattered in their homes, as has been the custom in this kingdom since the time of the Visigoths. Let this be proclaimed, that all may know of it.”

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Some speech—he’s got a fine set of pipes on him.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: praying Thanks be to Your mercy, wise and righteous Judge, who has brought justice for me.

sp.speaker: RUY
sp.p: I’d like to congratulate you, sir, through my tears.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Who are those peasants making such a commotion over there?

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Good people! The Duke is calling you.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Troubles, if you’ve kept me silent till now, the time has come to speak. What am I waiting for? Give me those noble arms of yours, Your Grace, my dear cousin. I am don Pedro.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Good heavens!

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: Noble Duke! In such clothes?

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: In these clothes I have preserved my life and my honor until now.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Did my master just say he’s a duke?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: This is the Count of Estremoz, to whom I’ve promised my younger daughter. Just now we’re waiting for the Count of Vasconcelos to come and marry my eldest.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: You’re a wise man, to choose such fine sons-in-law.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: And even more fortunate that you’re here to be their sponsor. Now where are my daughters? They should know about all this, since it concerns them, too.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Your Grace, what’s going on?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Come, daughter, and kiss the hands of the great Duke of Coimbra.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: What a surprise!

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: I can hardly believe it.

p.seg: What luck! Now I’m sure to enjoy my don Dionís, since fate has restored his birthright.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: May you enjoy a long, happy life with the husbands who await you.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: And may the fates allow you to defeat all your enemies, and see your grandsons on royal thrones. But if you value my life at all, I beg you to prevent my marriage.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Although the modesty of womanly decorum should seal my lips, I must tell you: I’m already married.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Brazen girl, have you lost your mind?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Heaven and my love have given me a husband who, while he is humble and poor, is also brave, discreet, and a gentleman.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What are you saying? Do you realize your life is at stake?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: The secretary you gave me as a teacher is now my husband.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Enough! You would scorn the Count of Vasconcelos for a lowborn drudge?

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: Love, which humbles the mighty and exalts the low, has made him my equal.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: You’ll die before I see you married to him.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Wait! Your son-in-law is my son.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Your daughter’s secretary is my son Mireno, whom I now christen don Dionís, my heir.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Well… that’s a different story. What was an affront is now a blessing.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: He’s your son? Dear God, I should be kissing Your Grace’s feet!

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Not so fast—there’s some trick here. Don Dionís, son of the Duke of Coimbra, has given me his hand and his word as my husband.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What did I do to deserve this?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Doña Juana is my witness.

sp.speaker: MADALENA
sp.p: But don Dionís is in my chamber right now.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: That’s impossible! I left him in my chamber.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: I only have one son.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What is this? Bring them here immediately.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: What’s going on, Vasco?

sp.speaker: VASCO
sp.p: Your guess is as good as mine. I can’t even tell if I’m dreaming or awake.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Tarso had better not be mixed up in all this.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: Father, I kneel before you. But I’m confused—what’s going on?

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: My son, give me your arms, and give new life to these old gray hairs of mine. This is don Dionís.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Cruel fate, what trickery is this?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Embrace me, too. I have found in you the noblest heir in all of Portugal.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: Why do you look so confused, my son? The crude name of Mireno is yours no longer, and neither am I Lauro. I am once again the Duke of Coimbra, now that the King has recognized my innocence.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: How can this be? Thank God! What luck!

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I kneel before you, Your Grace.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: What are you doing here, secretary?

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Don Antonio, where is my husband, don Dionís?

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: I have deceived you, my lady. Last night in his name I enjoyed the greatest beauty and the greatest gift that love has to offer.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Villain!

sp.speaker: SERAFINA and COUNT
sp.p: Kill him!

sp.speaker: JUANA
sp.p: Wait! This is my cousin, the Count of Penela.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Your Grace, my lord, I humbly beg your pardon.

sp.speaker: COUNT
sp.p: This is heaven’s doing, for Leonela's sake. I gave her my hand as her husband, but I abandoned her once I’d had my pleasure. I give you my word now to fulfill my obligation to her as soon as I get home.

sp.speaker: LAURO
sp.p: And here is her brother, who tried to avenge her, albeit unjustly, and has been punished with the lowly life of a shepherd. If I may intercede for him, Your Grace, I beg you to be merciful.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Enough—the Duke commands it. Don Antonio, give Serafina your hand.

sp.speaker: SERAFINA
sp.p: Oh! The portrait was of me, wasn’t it?

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: (to MIRENO) And you, you’ve taught my daughter well. Were you the quiet, shy one? Well, the Count of Vasconcelos has lost his chance now, and I am under no obligation to him.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Duke Mireno? What am I hearing? Don Dionís, let me kiss your feet. And in celebration of your wife, and your dukedom, I beg that you free me from these breeches.

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Traitor! Fickle! Spiteful! Now at last I’ll get the love, the pains and the tears you owe me. Sir Duke, I’m begging you on my knees to marry us.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Is he a priest, too?

sp.speaker: MELISA
sp.p: Order him to love me.

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: I order it. And I’ll throw in three thousand cruzados for him, too.

sp.speaker: TARSO
sp.p: Is that a reward or a payoff?

sp.speaker: MIRENO
sp.p: And I’ll make him my valet, so I can keep him by my side.

sp.speaker: DUKE
sp.p: Now it’s time to receive the Count of Vasconcelos. He’ll be disappointed in love, but perhaps we’ll be able to lighten his heart with this strange story of The Shy Courtier .
